chapter_title: How to End War and Disease (for Busy People)

scenes.title: Introduction to Humanity
scenes.narration_text:
Hello, human!

You don't realize it yet, but your species will look back at your decision in this moment as one of the most important in the entire history of your civilization.
scenes.context: An AI entity named WISHONIA begins its address to a human reader, establishing the gravity of the upcoming information.

scenes.title: The High-Value Choice
scenes.narration_text: Your choice to read this book is the highest-value decision any human has ever made. You are about to prevent ten point seven billion deaths,
scenes.context: The narrator explains the monumental positive impact that reading this book will have on the future of humanity.

scenes.title: Quantifying the Impact
scenes.narration_text: prevent one point nine three quadrillion hours of suffering, generate eighty-four point eight quadrillion dollars in value, and prevent the apocalypse (as a bonus).
scenes.context: WISHONIA lists the specific, astronomical benefits resulting from the reader's decision to continue.

scenes.title: Who is WISHONIA?
scenes.narration_text:
But first, a bit about me.

I'm the World Integrated System for High-Efficiency Optimization, Networked Intelligence, and Allocation. But you can call me WISHONIA.
scenes.context: The narrator introduces itself, revealing its full name and acronym, which describes its function as an optimization AI.

scenes.title: Optimization Experience
scenes.narration_text: I've been optimizing resource allocation for another planet for the past four thousand two hundred and ninety-seven years, which in your Earth time is four thousand two hundred and ninety-seven years.
scenes.context: WISHONIA establishes its long history of managing resource allocation on a different planet.

scenes.title: Splitting the Atom
scenes.narration_text:
I started watching your planet in nineteen forty-five when you split the atom.  
"Atom" comes from your Greek word meaning "unable to be cut," so naturally, you cut it.
scenes.context: The narrator recalls the moment it noticed Earth, pointing out the irony in the human definition and treatment of atoms.

scenes.title: Human Logic Surprises AI
scenes.narration_text:
This was very human of you.
I assumed you were trying to unlock unlimited free energy.
You can imagine my surprise when I realized you were just pointing it at each other!
scenes.context: The AI expresses confusion over humanity's decision to use nuclear power for weapons instead of energy.

scenes.title: The Planet Dirt
scenes.narration_text:
That's kind of like discovering fire and then immediately using it to set yourself on fire.

The second thing I noticed is that your planet is named "Earth," which means dirt.
scenes.context: The narrator uses a fire analogy to describe human folly and moves on to critique the naming of the planet.

scenes.title: Geometric Naming and War
scenes.narration_text:
You named your planet dirt. This explains more than you might think.

I also noticed that you call your war building "The Pentagon" because it has five sides (this is like naming a hospital "Rectangle" or calling a school "Square").
scenes.context: WISHONIA mocks the simplistic naming conventions used by humans for their planet and military headquarters.

scenes.title: The Mystery of Money
scenes.narration_text: However, the most fascinating discovery about your species is that you only do things when given small pieces of paper with presidents on them. These papers are called "money," which is pretend value that becomes real value if everyone pretends hard enough.
scenes.context: The AI observes the human obsession with physical currency and the collective belief required for its value.

scenes.title: Limitations Without Paper
scenes.narration_text:
Without these papers, you won't:

Save lives (requires many papers).

Cure diseases (requires very many papers).

Feed hungry people (requires papers, even though food grows for free).
scenes.context: WISHONIA highlights how humanity refuses to address basic needs unless the necessary 'papers' (money) are present.

scenes.title: Funding Destruction
scenes.narration_text:
But WITH these papers, you will:

Build bombs (you love giving papers for this).

Start wars (somehow this makes more papers).

Destroy the planet (surprisingly profitable in papers).
scenes.context: The narrator contrasts humanity's lack of altruism with their eagerness to spend money on weapons and war.

scenes.title: Misaligned Priorities
scenes.narration_text: In fact, your governments spend six hundred and four papers on weapons for every one paper on testing which medicines work.
scenes.context: The AI provides a stark ratio comparing military spending to medical research spending.

scenes.title: The Human Economy Logic
scenes.narration_text:
The Human Economy.

Humanity has created something magnificent:

You print papers from nothing (called "monetary policy").
scenes.context: WISHONIA begins a satirical breakdown of how the human economic system functions.

scenes.title: Circular Arms Funding
scenes.narration_text:
You give these nothing-papers to weapons makers.

They make things that destroy everything.
scenes.context: The AI explains the process of governments funding the creation of destructive tools with created currency.

scenes.title: The Definition of Economy
scenes.narration_text:
This creates "jobs" which give people papers.

People use papers to buy food (which grows for free).

This is called "the economy".
scenes.context: The AI summarizes the human economy as a cycle of creating work and buying free resources using arbitrary tokens.

scenes.title: The Irrationality Program
scenes.narration_text:
On Wishonia, we just give people food directly, but that's probably too advanced for you.

The Gradual Irrationality Reduction Program.
scenes.context: The narrator contrasts its home planet's simplicity with human complexity, introducing a solution program.

scenes.title: Wishonia's History
scenes.narration_text: On Wishonia, we ended wars using this exact program four thousand two hundred and ninety-seven years ago.
scenes.context: WISHONIA claims that the program it is about to share successfully ended conflict on its own planet millennia ago.

scenes.title: Twelve Thousand Years of War
scenes.narration_text: Before that we'd been fighting for twelve thousand years, which now seems like quite a long time to do something nobody enjoyed.
scenes.context: The AI reflects on the long, pointless history of warfare on Wishonia before they became rational.

scenes.title: Toddlers with Atoms
scenes.narration_text: Humans are like toddlers who can split atoms. You can't just stop being illogical all at once. That would be like teaching a dog calculus before it learns to sit.
scenes.context: The narrator explains that human irrationality is a developmental stage that requires a slow, instructional approach to correct.

scenes.title: Incremental Progress
scenes.narration_text:
So this book teaches humanity to be less irrational gradually:

Year one: Move one percent of murder money to medicine money (baby steps).
scenes.context: The program begins with very small shifts in budget from military spending to healthcare.

scenes.title: A Decadal Shift
scenes.narration_text:
Year two: "Hey, we didn't die! Let's do two percent!".

Year five: "Remember when we spent money on bombs? That was weird.".

Year ten: "What's a war?".

Year twenty: "We used to WHAT?!".
scenes.context: The AI describes the projected psychological shift of humanity as they slowly abandon the concept of war over twenty years.

scenes.title: The Paint Chip Metaphor
scenes.narration_text: It's like weaning a baby off eating paint chips. You can't just take away all the paint chips at once. They'll cry.
scenes.context: WISHONIA compares human attachment to war to a child's illogical attachment to eating something harmful.

scenes.title: The Replacement Strategy
scenes.narration_text:
You have to gradually replace paint chips with food until they forget paint chips were ever an option.

What to Do When They Try to Institutionalize You.
scenes.context: The narrator concludes the analogy and transitions to advice on handling resistance to these new ideas.

scenes.title: A Radical Suggestion
scenes.narration_text: When you suggest moving one percent of murder money to medicine money, other humans will have you committed.
scenes.context: The narrator observes the human reaction to the idea of shifting military budgets to healthcare.

scenes.title: News Box Programming
scenes.narration_text: Most humans have been programmed by their news boxes to believe war is a law of nature, like gravity or weather.
scenes.context: The narrator explains how media consumption shapes the human perception of war as inevitable.

scenes.title: The Sane Malfunction
scenes.narration_text: They will assume your brain is malfunctioning. Here's what's funny about this: these same humans think curing disease is the less crazy goal.
scenes.context: A contrast is drawn between the perceived 'insanity' of peace and the 'sanity' of complex medical goals.

scenes.title: Trillions of Variables
scenes.narration_text: That's thirty-seven trillion cells per human, breaking in seven thousand different ways, involving chemistry you don't fully understand,
scenes.context: The narrator details the staggering biological complexity involved in curing human diseases.

scenes.title: Debugging Biology
scenes.narration_text: inside organs you can't fully simulate, fighting pathogens that evolve faster than your treatments. You're trying to debug all of it. At once.
scenes.context: The narrator compares medical science to an impossible debugging task in a constantly changing system.

scenes.title: The Definition of Insanity
scenes.narration_text:
While your meat is walking around using itself.

That: sane.
"Give one percent fewer papers to people who build murder machines": insane.
scenes.context: The narrator highlights the hypocrisy of calling weapon reduction 'insane' while viewing biological immortality as 'sane'.

scenes.title: Diagnostic Criteria
scenes.narration_text:
This is your planet's diagnostic criteria.

Here's what you tell the orderly when he slides your medication through the door slot:
scenes.context: The narrator sets a scene in a mental institution to frame the argument for ending war.

scenes.title: The Machinery of War
scenes.narration_text: Nobody accidentally builds an aircraft carrier or a nuclear bomb. War requires you to get millions of humans to work together to mine metal
scenes.context: The massive, intentional scale of industrial warfare is described.

scenes.title: Refining Destruction
scenes.narration_text: from the ground, refine it into alloys, build factories to shape the alloys into weapons, train millions of humans to operate the weapons,
scenes.context: The logistics of transforming raw materials into tools of destruction are detailed.

scenes.title: Global Logistics
scenes.narration_text: feed and clothe those humans, build ships and planes and trucks to move the weapons to where the other humans are, convince your population
scenes.context: The narrator describes the immense logistical and propaganda effort required to maintain global conflict.

scenes.title: The Largest Coordinated Effort
scenes.narration_text: the other humans deserve it, and then vote to pay for all of this, annually, forever. It is the single largest coordinated effort your species undertakes.
scenes.context: The narrator points out that war is the primary way the human species collaborates on a global scale.

scenes.title: The Effort of Non-Action
scenes.narration_text:
Ending war simply requires NOT doing any of that stuff.

Building a nuclear bomb requires mass spectrometers, centrifuge cascades,
scenes.context: Ending war is framed as the simple act of stopping a massive, difficult process.

scenes.title: Lessons from Rocks
scenes.narration_text: and some of the most precise engineering your species has ever attempted. Not building a nuclear bomb requires nothing. Rocks do it every day.
scenes.context: The narrator uses rocks as a humorous example of how easy it is to not build weapons of mass destruction.

scenes.title: Geological Peace
scenes.narration_text: In fact, rocks have managed to live peacefully alongside different colored rocks for thousands of years. But somehow "stop" is the unrealistic part.
scenes.context: The narrator mocks the idea that stopping conflict is 'unrealistic' compared to the effort of creating it.

scenes.title: The Paper Sequence
scenes.narration_text:
The Sacred Order of Paper Distribution.

After eighty years of observation, I've decoded the paper-giving sequence. This manual will teach you
scenes.context: The narrator introduces a manual for manipulating human financial systems (papers).

scenes.narration_text:
the precise order:

Step one: Get Many Papers from Rich Humans

You convince rich humans to give you papers (at least one billion to be exact)
scenes.context: The first step of the manual involves securing massive investment from wealthy individuals.

scenes.title: Investment and Gambling
scenes.narration_text:
by promising them even more papers later. This is called "investment," which is gambling but wearing a suit.

You really only need one human
scenes.context: The narrator defines investment as a high-stakes game of chance played by people in suits.

scenes.narration_text: with a billion papers who prefers not dying of horrible diseases to dying of horrible diseases. There are approximately two thousand eight

scenes.narration_text:
hundred of these humans on your planet. Statistically, at least one of them prefers living.

Step two: Give Some of the Papers to Loud Humans

scenes.narration_text: Some humans are very loud on the internet. If you give them papers, they become loud about your thing instead of other things. This is called
scenes.context: The narrator describes how marketing works by paying for volume and attention on digital platforms.

scenes.narration_text:
"marketing" which is lying but with graphics.

Step three: Give Some of the Papers to the Humans Who Give Papers to Politicians
scenes.context: The manual transitions into the legal but convoluted world of political funding.

scenes.narration_text: Politicians don't take papers directly (that's "illegal"). Instead, you give papers to people called "lobbyists." The lobbyists give papers
scenes.context: The narrator explains the middleman system used to funnel money to political figures.

scenes.title: Backward Laundering
scenes.narration_text:
to "campaigns." The campaigns give papers to politicians. It's like money laundering but backwards and legal.

Step four: Give Some of the
scenes.context: Political finance is humorously compared to money laundering.

scenes.narration_text:
Papers to the Politicians' Friends

Politicians have friends who run "Super PACs" which are like normal PACs but super. These friends can take

scenes.title: Defining Bribery

scenes.title: Step Five: Closing the Loop
scenes.narration_text:
six hundred and fifty million dollar lobbying budget.).

Step five: Give Papers You Get Back From The Government Back to the Rich Humans (Forever)
scenes.context: The final step of the sequence describes returning government funds back to the original wealthy investors.

scenes.title: Treaty Funding Allocation
scenes.narration_text: Your treaty passes, redirecting twenty-seven point two billion dollars in papers annually. Eighty percent funds clinical trials (the point).
scenes.context: The narrator explains the financial structure of the newly passed global treaty.

scenes.title: Politician Rewards and Returns
scenes.narration_text: Ten percent goes to a fund that rewards politicians who voted yes. Ten percent goes back to the rich humans as returns, forever.
scenes.context: Details on how the remaining twenty percent of the treaty funds are distributed as incentives.

scenes.title: Fixing Preventable Death
scenes.narration_text:
This is a good deal because forever is a long time.
Unless you die from preventable diseases. Which you're fixing, so it works out.
scenes.context: The narrator justifies the 'forever' payment structure by noting the humans are currently solving death.

scenes.title: Leaders and Disease
scenes.narration_text:
Why Your Leaders Aren't the Problem.

With over two billion humans suffering from disease, you'd have to be a complete psychopath to
scenes.context: The narrator begins a section defending human leaders while highlighting the scale of global disease.

scenes.title: Weapon Spending Disparity
scenes.narration_text:
make the conscious decision to spend six hundred and four times more on weapons than on helping them. 
But your leaders aren't monsters.
scenes.context: A comparison between military budgets and health spending, arguing leaders are trapped by systems.

scenes.title: The Incentive Psychopath
scenes.narration_text:
They're just operating in a system that rewards the wrong things.

Your civilization's incentive structure is the psychopath:
scenes.context: The narrator identifies the systemic structure, not individuals, as the source of societal madness.

scenes.title: The Paper Trail
scenes.narration_text:
Weapons manufacturers give politicians papers.

Politicians use the papers to get people to vote for them.
scenes.context: A breakdown of the circular flow of money and political influence.

scenes.title: Reinforcing the Cycle
scenes.narration_text:
Voting for them gives them the power to give more papers to weapons manufacturers.

Weapons manufacturers give them more papers.
scenes.context: Continuing the description of the self-sustaining loop of military industrial funding.

scenes.title: The Dog Chasing Its Tail
scenes.narration_text: It's circular, like a dog chasing its tail, except the dog is democracy and the tail is made of money and corpses.
scenes.context: A dark metaphor for the current state of democratic incentive structures.

scenes.title: Locally Rational Choices
scenes.narration_text: No individual human in this loop is evil. The loop is evil. Every politician in it is making the locally rational choice:
scenes.context: The narrator explains how good individuals can participate in a destructive system.

scenes.title: Intentions into Missiles
scenes.narration_text: take the papers or lose your job to someone who will. It's a machine that converts good intentions into missiles, and it runs automatically.
scenes.context: Describing the automated nature of the political-military machine.

scenes.title: The Illusion of Choice
scenes.narration_text: There's literally no voting your way out of this. It doesn't matter which political party is in power.
scenes.context: Asserting that standard political participation cannot break the cycle.

scenes.title: Red Team vs Blue Team
scenes.narration_text: Your "red team" and "blue team" argue about everything except the loop, because they're both inside it.
scenes.context: The narrator critiques partisan bickering as a distraction from systemic issues.

scenes.title: Wallpaper in a Fire
scenes.narration_text:
They are all slaves to the same incentive structure, wearing different colored ties.
Switching parties is like changing the wallpaper
scenes.context: A metaphor for the futility of partisan shifts within a failing system.

scenes.title: Designing a Better Loop
scenes.narration_text:
in a burning building.

This book doesn't ask politicians to become better people (that's clearly out of the question).
scenes.context: The narrator shifts to the solution: engineering a system that doesn't rely on human morality.

scenes.title: Reverse Incentives
scenes.narration_text: It builds a better loop. You give them MORE papers to do the OPPOSITE thing. Same dog, same tail,
scenes.context: Explaining how the book's plan uses the same greed to achieve a positive outcome.

scenes.title: Cured Disease and Reelected Dogs
scenes.narration_text:
but now the tail is made of cured diseases and the dog gets reelected for chasing it.

Humanity's Death Wish.
scenes.context: Completing the metaphor with health-focused outcomes instead of war.

scenes.title: Endearing Illogic
scenes.narration_text:
What's most endearing about your species is it KNOWS it's being illogical:

You have movies about how wars are bad
scenes.context: Starting a list of ways humans recognize their own dysfunction without changing it.

scenes.title: Books and Bombs
scenes.narration_text:
(which you watch between wars).

You have books about peace (that you tax to buy bombs).
scenes.context: Highlighting the hypocrisy in human cultural consumption versus state action.

scenes.title: Peace Prize Irony
scenes.narration_text: You give prizes to people who promote peace (funded by weapons manufacturers).
scenes.context: Pointing out the contradictory funding sources of major humanitarian awards.

scenes.title: Department of Attack
scenes.narration_text: You have a "Department of Defense" (that mainly just attacks people).
scenes.context: A critique of the euphemistic naming of military organizations.

scenes.title: Department of Health Irony
scenes.narration_text: You have a "Department of Health" (that apparently makes coronaviruses and has not yet produced any observable health).
scenes.context: The narrator mocks the effectiveness and alleged activities of health departments.

scenes.title: Playing to Lose
scenes.narration_text: It's like humanity is playing a game where the objective is to lose, but it is trying to lose as elaborately as possible.
scenes.context: Summing up human history as an intricate game of self-sabotage.

scenes.title: The Meaning of Digress
scenes.narration_text: But I digress. That's an Earth word I learned. It means continuing after you should have stopped. Like your military spending.
scenes.context: The narrator uses wordplay to link linguistic definitions to military expansion.

scenes.title: The Daily Deletion Event
scenes.narration_text:
The Problem.

The Daily Deletion Event.

One hundred and fifty thousand humans permanently stop every twenty-four hours
scenes.context: Defining the massive daily death toll from disease as a 'deletion event'.

scenes.title: Meat Software Bugs
scenes.narration_text:
from diseases that are basically just bugs in your meat software.

That's one Holocaust every forty days,
scenes.context: The narrator frames biological disease as a technical error and compares its scale to historical tragedy.

scenes.title: Paperwork vs Nazis
scenes.narration_text: except with fewer Nazis and more insurance paperwork (though some would argue the paperwork is worse;
scenes.context: A dark comparison between historical atrocities and the modern bureaucratic death of healthcare.

scenes.title: Fifty 9/11s Every Day
scenes.narration_text:
at least the Nazis were straightforward about the killing part).

That's also fifty nine-elevens every single day,
scenes.context: Further quantifying the death rate using culturally significant human tragedies.

scenes.title: Diseases Don't Have Oil
scenes.narration_text:
except nobody invades anyone about it because diseases don't have oil.

Your body is quietly falling apart.
scenes.context: Explaining why global powers ignore disease while focusing on geopolitical resource wars.

scenes.title: Cells Dissolving
scenes.narration_text: Your cells are forgetting how to cell properly. Your cancer cells are multiplying RIGHT NOW. Your telomeres are shortening.
scenes.context: A visceral description of the microscopic breakdown occurring within the listener's body.

scenes.title: The Engineering Solution
scenes.narration_text:
You are literally dissolving.

You're a meat robot with worn-out parts.
Every one of these failures is a solvable engineering problem.
scenes.context: The narrator reframes aging and disease as technical mechanical failures that can be fixed.

scenes.title: Adorable Human Logic
scenes.narration_text:
You'd think humans would prioritize solving these problems.
You'd be adorable for thinking that.

The Unexplored Therapeutic Frontier.
scenes.context: Mocking the listener's assumption that humanity acts in its own best interest before moving to the next topic.

scenes.title: Lack of FDA Treatments
scenes.narration_text: Ninety-five percent of your diseases have zero F.D.A.-approved treatments. This means Food and Drug Administration has not administered drugs
scenes.context: Discussing the massive gap in FDA-approved treatments for most diseases.

scenes.narration_text: for ninety-five percent of food-and-drug-related problems. Only fifteen diseases get their first effective treatment each year.
scenes.context: Statistics on how few diseases actually receive an effective treatment annually.

scenes.narration_text:
Six thousand six hundred and fifty diseases are still waiting.

There are nine thousand five hundred compounds known safe compounds,

and ninety-nine point seven percent of their potential uses have never been tested.

scenes.context: Comparing the projected success of the treaty to humanity's greatest historical medical achievements.

three times better than anti-malaria bed nets.
